specStatements.text: When a current flows through a conducting wire a magnetic field is produced around the wire. The strength of the magnetic field depends on the current through the wire and the distance from the wire.
Shaping a wire to form a solenoid increases the strength of the magnetic field created by a current through the wire. The magnetic field inside a solenoid is strong and uniform.

The magnetic field around a solenoid has a similar shape to that of a bar magnet. Adding an iron core increases the strength of the magnetic field of a solenoid. An electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core.
Students should be able to:
• describe how the magnetic effect of a current can be demonstrated
• draw the magnetic field pattern for a straight wire carrying a current and for a solenoid (showing the direction of the field)
• explain how a solenoid arrangement can increase the magnetic effect of the current.
(Physics only) Students should be able to interpret diagrams of electromagnetic devices in order to explain how they work.
When a conductor carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other. This is called the motor effect.
Students should be able to show that Fleming's left-hand rule represents the relative orientation of the force, the current in the conductor and the magnetic field.
Students should be able to recall the factors that affect the size of the force on the conductor.
For a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field and carrying a current:
force = magnetic flux density × current × length
[F = B I l]
force, F, in newtons, N
magnetic flux density, B, in tesla, T
current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere)
length, l, in metres, m
A coil of wire carrying a current in a magnetic field tends to rotate. This is the basis of an electric motor.
Students should be able to explain how t he force on a conductor in a magnetic field causes the rotation of the coil in an electric motor.
Loudspeakers and headphones use the motor effect to convert variations in current in electrical circuits to the pressure variations in sound waves.
Students should be able to explain how a moving-coil loudspeaker and headphones work.

scopeNotes.statement: For a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field and carrying a current:
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The equation force = magnetic flux density × current × length is stated and used only for a conductor at right angles to the field. Every calculation in this section (q16, q18) states that the conductor is at right angles, and no item asks for a force at any other angle. Where a conductor lies along the field (q12) the material states that the force is zero rather than resolving components or introducing an angle factor; no version of the equation containing sinθ appears anywhere in this content.

concepts.term: Magnetic effect of a current
concepts.definition: Whenever a current flows in a conducting wire, a magnetic field is produced in the space around the wire. The field exists only while the current flows; switch the current off and the field disappears. This is the magnetic effect of a current.

concepts.term: Magnetic field pattern around a straight wire
concepts.definition: The field lines around a long straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles lying in a plane at right angles to the wire, centred on the wire. The circles are drawn closest together near the wire and further apart as the distance from the wire increases, showing that the field is strongest close to the wire.

concepts.term: Factors affecting the field strength around a wire
concepts.definition: The strength of the magnetic field around a straight wire depends on two things only: the current through the wire (a larger current gives a stronger field) and the distance from the wire (the field gets weaker as you move further away).

concepts.term: Direction of the field around a wire (right-hand grip rule)
concepts.definition: The specification requires the field pattern to be drawn showing the direction of the field. Grip the wire with the right hand so that the thumb points along the conventional current; the curled fingers then give the direction of the circular field lines. Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field lines but not their circular shape.

concepts.term: Solenoid
concepts.definition: A solenoid is a wire wound into a long coil of many turns. Shaping a wire this way increases the strength of the magnetic field created by a current through the wire, because the fields due to the individual turns add together inside the coil.

concepts.term: Uniform field inside a solenoid
concepts.definition: The magnetic field inside a solenoid is strong and uniform: it has the same strength and the same direction at every point inside the coil. On a diagram this is shown by straight, parallel, evenly spaced field lines running along the inside of the solenoid.

concepts.term: Field around a solenoid
concepts.definition: Outside the coil, the magnetic field around a solenoid has a similar shape to that of a bar magnet: the lines emerge from one end (the north pole), loop round through the space outside and return to the other end (the south pole). Swapping the direction of the current swaps the poles.

concepts.term: Iron core
concepts.definition: A core of iron placed inside a solenoid increases the strength of the magnetic field of the solenoid. Iron is used because it is magnetically soft: it magnetises strongly while the current flows and loses almost all of its magnetism when the current is switched off.

concepts.term: Electromagnet
concepts.definition: An electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core. Because its field is produced by a current, an electromagnet can be switched on and off, and its strength can be changed by changing the current. This is what distinguishes it from a permanent magnet.

concepts.term: Demonstrating the magnetic effect of a current
concepts.definition: The magnetic effect can be demonstrated by placing plotting compasses around a wire and switching the current on: the compass needles swing to line up with the circular field and swing the other way when the current is reversed. Iron filings sprinkled on a card through which the wire passes settle into the circular pattern. Attraction of steel paper clips by a current-carrying coil is a further demonstration.

concepts.term: Why a solenoid increases the magnetic effect
concepts.definition: Each turn of the coil produces its own circular field. Inside the solenoid, the fields of all the turns point the same way and add together, so the more turns there are in a given length, the stronger the resultant field. Increasing the current or adding an iron core strengthens it further.

concepts.term: Interpreting diagrams of electromagnetic devices (Physics only)
concepts.definition: To explain a device from its diagram, trace the sequence: current in a coil creates a magnetic field, the field magnetises an iron part, and the resulting attraction (or the loss of it when the current stops) produces the movement the device needs. Switching the current off removes the field, so the moving part returns.

concepts.term: Relay (worked example of an electromagnetic device)
concepts.definition: In a relay, a small current in a coil makes an electromagnet. The electromagnet attracts a pivoted iron armature, which pushes a pair of contacts together and completes a second, high-current circuit. When the small current stops, the field collapses and a spring pulls the contacts apart. A relay therefore lets a small, safe current switch a large one.

concepts.term: The motor effect
concepts.definition: When a conductor carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field, the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other. This is called the motor effect. The force acts on both objects, not just on the wire, because the two magnetic fields interact.

concepts.term: Fleming's left-hand rule
concepts.definition: Hold the thumb and the first two fingers of the LEFT hand at right angles to one another. The First finger points along the magnetic Field (north to south), the seCond finger points along the Conventional Current, and the thuMb then gives the direction of the force (the Motion). The rule shows the relative orientation of force, current and field: each is at right angles to the other two.

concepts.term: Factors affecting the size of the force
concepts.definition: The size of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field depends on the magnetic flux density of the field, the current through the conductor, and the length of conductor that is in the field. It also depends on the orientation of the conductor in the field: the force is greatest when the conductor is at right angles to the field and zero when it lies along the field.

concepts.term: Conductor at right angles to the field
concepts.definition: The equation force = magnetic flux density x current x length applies to a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field and carrying a current. If the conductor is turned so that it lies along the field lines, there is no force on it at all.

concepts.term: The equation force = magnetic flux density x current x length
concepts.definition: For a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field and carrying a current: force = magnetic flux density x current x length, written in symbols as F = B I l. This equation is supplied on the Physics equation sheet in the exam, so it does not have to be recalled, but it must be selected, rearranged and applied correctly, with all quantities in the units the specification gives.

concepts.term: Magnetic flux density
concepts.definition: Magnetic flux density, symbol B, measures how strong a magnetic field is; it is measured in tesla, T. One tesla is the flux density that gives a force of 1 N on a 1 m length of conductor carrying a current of 1 A at right angles to the field.

concepts.term: Quantities and units in F = B I l
concepts.definition: force, F, in newtons, N; magnetic flux density, B, in tesla, T; current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere); length, l, in metres, m. A length given in centimetres must be converted to metres before the equation is used.

concepts.term: Turning effect on a coil in a magnetic field
concepts.definition: A coil of wire carrying a current in a magnetic field tends to rotate. The current runs in opposite directions along the two opposite sides of the coil, so by Fleming's left-hand rule the forces on those two sides act in opposite directions: one side is pushed up and the other down. This pair of forces turns the coil, and it is the basis of an electric motor.

concepts.term: Split-ring commutator
concepts.definition: Half a turn after the coil starts to rotate, the two sides have swapped over, so the forces would turn the coil back again. The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, so the force on each side keeps pushing the coil the same way round and the rotation continues.

concepts.term: Moving-coil loudspeaker
concepts.definition: A loudspeaker has a coil attached to a paper or plastic cone, sitting in the field of a permanent magnet. A varying current in the coil produces a varying force on it by the motor effect, so the coil and cone move in and out in step with the current. The moving cone pushes on the air, producing the pressure variations of a sound wave.

concepts.term: Headphones
concepts.definition: Headphones work in the same way as a loudspeaker but on a much smaller scale: a small coil in the field of a permanent magnet is driven by the varying current and moves a small diaphragm, converting variations in current in electrical circuits to the pressure variations in sound waves close to the ear.

misconceptions.question: What is the shape of the magnetic field pattern around a long straight wire carrying a current?
misconceptions.correct: The field lines are circles centred on the wire, lying in a plane at right angles to the wire.
misconceptions.misconception: The field lines shoot straight outwards from the wire in all directions, like the spokes of a wheel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet radial patterns first, in diagrams of light spreading from a lamp and of gravitational or electric fields around a point, and reuse that picture here.
misconceptions.correction: Plotting compasses placed around the wire do not point away from it; they line up end-to-end around it, tracing closed circles. Magnetic field lines are always closed loops and never start or end on the wire.

misconceptions.question: A compass is moved from 2 cm to 6 cm away from a wire carrying a steady current. What happens to the field strength at the compass?
misconceptions.correct: It gets weaker, because the strength of the field depends on the distance from the wire as well as on the current.
misconceptions.misconception: It stays the same, because the current has not changed and the current is what sets the field strength.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The current is the quantity the student has been asked about most often, so distance is treated as irrelevant scenery rather than as a variable.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the strength of the magnetic field depends on the current through the wire AND the distance from the wire. On a field diagram the circles are drawn further apart further out, which is exactly how a weaker field is shown.

misconceptions.question: In which direction do the magnetic field lines around a straight wire point?
misconceptions.correct: They point around the wire, in circles at right angles to it; the direction of the circles is given by the right-hand grip rule.
misconceptions.misconception: They point along the wire, in the same direction as the current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Current has a direction along the wire, and students carry that single direction over to the field instead of treating the field as a separate quantity with its own geometry.
misconceptions.correction: The field is at right angles to the current everywhere. Grip the wire with the right hand, thumb along the conventional current, and the fingers curl the way the field lines run.

misconceptions.question: The current in a wire is reversed. What happens to the magnetic field around it?
misconceptions.correct: The field lines keep their circular shape, but their direction reverses.
misconceptions.misconception: Nothing changes, because the field just depends on how big the current is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Field strength and field direction get merged into one idea, and since the size of the current has not changed the student concludes nothing has changed.
misconceptions.correction: A plotting compass beside the wire visibly swings through 180 degrees when the current is reversed. Reversing the current reverses the field direction; this is why a motor reverses when its supply is reversed.

misconceptions.question: Is the magnetic field around a straight wire the same strength everywhere?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is strongest close to the wire and gets weaker with distance from the wire.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes, the field around a wire is uniform, the same everywhere around it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word uniform is learned for the inside of a solenoid and then applied to any current-carrying wire.
misconceptions.correction: Uniform describes the field inside a solenoid, not the field around a straight wire. Around a wire the field falls away with distance, which is why the circles on a field diagram get further apart.

misconceptions.question: What do the field lines look like inside a solenoid?
misconceptions.correct: They are straight, parallel and evenly spaced, running along the axis of the coil: a strong, uniform field.
misconceptions.misconception: They are circles inside the coil, the same as the circles around a single straight wire.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The field around one wire is learned first, and the solenoid is treated as that same wire bent round, so the circular pattern is imported unchanged.
misconceptions.correction: Inside the coil the circular fields of the separate turns line up and add along the axis. Iron filings inside a solenoid settle into straight lines along the coil, not rings.

misconceptions.question: What is the magnetic field like at the centre of a current-carrying solenoid?
misconceptions.correct: It is strong and uniform.
misconceptions.misconception: It is zero, because the fields from the turns on opposite sides of the coil cancel one another out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly notice that opposite sides of the coil carry current in opposite directions and wrongly conclude the fields must cancel, as forces on opposite sides of a coil do.
misconceptions.correction: On opposite sides of the coil the current flows in opposite directions, but those sides are also on opposite sides of the centre, so their circular fields point the SAME way through the middle and reinforce.

misconceptions.question: Why is the field of a solenoid stronger than the field of the same wire left straight?
misconceptions.correct: Because the magnetic fields produced by the many turns add together inside the coil.
misconceptions.misconception: Because coiling the wire lowers its resistance, so a bigger current flows.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any change to a circuit is assumed to work through current and resistance, the quantities used most in the electricity topic.
misconceptions.correction: Coiling a wire does not reduce its resistance; the same length of wire has the same resistance whatever its shape. The field is stronger because many turns contribute their fields to the same region.

misconceptions.question: Where does the extra magnetic field of a solenoid come from?
misconceptions.correct: From the fields of all the individual turns adding together in the space inside the coil.
misconceptions.misconception: The turns of the coil store magnetic field in the gaps between them and let it out later.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Magnetic field is treated as a substance that can be collected and stored, in the way charge is stored on a capacitor or energy in a store.
misconceptions.correction: A magnetic field is not a substance and is not stored. It exists only while the current flows and vanishes the instant the current stops.

misconceptions.question: Is there a magnetic field outside a solenoid?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Outside the coil the field has a similar shape to that of a bar magnet, looping from one end round to the other.
misconceptions.misconception: No. All the field is concentrated inside the coil, so outside there is nothing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The teaching emphasis on the strong uniform field inside the solenoid is read as meaning the field is only inside.
misconceptions.correction: Field lines are closed loops: whatever runs through the inside of the coil must return round the outside. That outside pattern is what makes a solenoid behave like a bar magnet.

misconceptions.question: An iron core is put inside a current-carrying solenoid. What has been made?
misconceptions.correct: An electromagnet: a solenoid with an iron core, whose field is stronger than that of the solenoid alone.
misconceptions.misconception: A permanent magnet, because the iron has been turned into a magnet.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The iron does become magnetised, and students who have met magnetising a steel bar assume the magnetism is permanent.
misconceptions.correction: The iron is magnetised only while the current flows; switch the current off and the field almost entirely disappears. That is precisely why the device is an electromagnet and not a permanent magnet.

misconceptions.question: What does the iron core do in an electromagnet?
misconceptions.correct: It increases the strength of the magnetic field of the solenoid.
misconceptions.misconception: It just holds the coil in shape; the field is the same with or without it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The core looks like a former or a support in diagrams, and its role is read as mechanical rather than magnetic.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that adding an iron core increases the strength of the magnetic field of a solenoid. An iron-cored coil will pick up far more paper clips than the same coil with a wooden rod or air inside it.

misconceptions.question: Does a solenoid have magnetic poles if it has no iron core?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A current-carrying solenoid has a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other, with or without a core.
misconceptions.misconception: No, it only has poles once an iron core is put in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Poles are associated with lumps of iron rather than with the field pattern, so a coil of wire on its own is not seen as a magnet.
misconceptions.correction: The poles come from the field pattern, which is produced by the current. An air-cored solenoid deflects a compass and attracts a magnet; the core only makes the same field stronger.

misconceptions.question: How can you show that a current produces a magnetic field?
misconceptions.correct: Place a plotting compass near the wire; the needle deflects when the current is switched on and deflects the other way when it is reversed.
misconceptions.misconception: Show that the wire gets warm when the current flows.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know a current has several effects and do not separate them, so any observable change in the wire is offered as evidence for whichever effect is being asked about.
misconceptions.correction: Warming is the heating effect, not the magnetic effect. The demonstration must involve something magnetic responding, such as a compass needle, iron filings or attracted steel clips.

misconceptions.question: Does showing that a current is flowing prove that a magnetic field is produced?
misconceptions.correct: No. To demonstrate the magnetic effect you must show a magnetic response, such as a compass needle deflecting.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes, if a lamp lights or an ammeter reads, that shows the wire is magnetic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The reasoning slips from a current always produces a field to any sign of current is a demonstration of the field, which confuses a fact with the evidence for it.
misconceptions.correction: A lit lamp shows only that charge is flowing. The demonstration has to make the field itself detectable, and that requires a magnetic detector next to the wire.

misconceptions.question: Which end of a current-carrying solenoid is the north pole?
misconceptions.correct: The end from which the field lines emerge, found from the direction of the current round the coil.
misconceptions.misconception: The end nearest the positive terminal, because current flows from the north pole to the south pole in a coil.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule that field lines run from north to south outside a magnet gets applied to the current instead of to the field.
misconceptions.correction: Current and field are different quantities. Looked at end-on, an anticlockwise current gives a north pole at that end and a clockwise current gives a south pole.

misconceptions.question: How do you decide which end of a solenoid is north?
misconceptions.correct: Look at the end face: if the conventional current runs anticlockwise, that end is north; if it runs clockwise, that end is south.
misconceptions.misconception: The north pole is at the end where the current enters the coil.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for a simple entry-and-exit rule rather than examining the direction the current circulates when viewed end-on.
misconceptions.correction: The pole depends on the sense in which the current circulates, not on which end of the wire is connected first. Winding the same coil the opposite way, with the same connections, swaps the poles.

misconceptions.question: How does a relay use a small current to switch on a large current?
misconceptions.correct: The small current makes an electromagnet, which attracts an iron armature and pushes a pair of contacts together in the second circuit.
misconceptions.misconception: The small current heats a strip of metal until it bends far enough to touch the contacts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The bimetallic strip is a familiar switching mechanism from thermostats and some circuit breakers, and is reached for whenever a switch operates by itself.
misconceptions.correction: A relay contains a coil and an iron armature, not a heater. Its action is magnetic and immediate, which is why a relay switches the instant the coil current flows.

misconceptions.question: Are the two circuits in a relay electrically connected?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are separate; the link between them is magnetic and mechanical, through the electromagnet and the armature.
misconceptions.misconception: The coil pushes current straight into the second circuit, which is how that circuit switches on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any coil in a diagram is read as passing electricity on to whatever is drawn next to it, especially once induction has been met.
misconceptions.correction: The whole point of a relay is that the circuits stay isolated: a small, safe current in one circuit operates a switch that carries a much larger current in the other.

misconceptions.question: A current-carrying wire is placed between the poles of a magnet. Which objects experience a force?
misconceptions.correct: Both. The magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the wire is pushed; the magnet feels nothing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The wire is the part seen to move in the classroom demonstration, because the magnet is heavy and often clamped, so students conclude only the wire is acted on.
misconceptions.correction: The forces are a Newton's third law pair. Rest the magnet on a top-pan balance and the reading changes when the current flows, showing the magnet is pushed just as hard the other way.

misconceptions.question: Must a wire be moving before the motor effect gives it a force?
misconceptions.correct: No. A stationary wire carrying a current in a magnetic field experiences a force straight away.
misconceptions.misconception: The wire has to be moving first, because movement is what produces the effect.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The motor effect is confused with electromagnetic induction, where relative movement is genuinely needed.
misconceptions.correction: In the motor effect the current is supplied and the force causes the motion. In induction the motion is supplied and a potential difference is the result; these are opposite processes.

misconceptions.question: When is the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field greatest?
misconceptions.correct: When the conductor is at right angles to the magnetic field.
misconceptions.misconception: When the conductor lies along the field lines, pointing the same way as the field.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture the wire and the field lines lining up as the arrangement in which they interact most, by analogy with two magnets attracting when placed end to end.
misconceptions.correction: The specification gives the equation for a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field. A conductor lying along the field lines experiences no force at all.

misconceptions.question: In what direction does the motor effect force act?
misconceptions.correct: At right angles to both the magnetic field and the current.
misconceptions.misconception: Along the field lines, in the direction the field points.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Force is associated with pushes and pulls along a line between magnets, as in attraction and repulsion, so students expect the force to lie along the field.
misconceptions.correction: Fleming's left-hand rule holds the thumb, first finger and second finger at right angles to one another precisely because the force is perpendicular to both the field and the current.

misconceptions.question: What does the thumb represent in Fleming's left-hand rule?
misconceptions.correct: The force, that is the direction of motion of the conductor.
misconceptions.misconception: The current, because the thumb comes first and current is what you are given first.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three-fingers arrangement is learned as a sequence of words without the F-F-C mnemonic linking each digit to its quantity.
misconceptions.correction: First finger Field, seCond finger Current, thuMb Motion or force. Assigning current to the thumb produces a force prediction at right angles to the true one.

misconceptions.question: Which finger shows the current in Fleming's left-hand rule?
misconceptions.correct: The second finger.
misconceptions.misconception: The first finger shows the current and the second finger shows the field.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two fingers carry similar-sounding roles and are easily swapped when the mnemonic is not used carefully.
misconceptions.correction: The First finger is the Field and the seCond finger is the Current; the initial letters are the memory aid. Swapping them reverses the predicted force.

misconceptions.question: Does it matter which hand is used for Fleming's rule?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The left hand is used for the motor effect.
misconceptions.misconception: Either hand works, as long as the fingers are at right angles.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two similar rules are taught close together, and students who have met the right-hand rule for induction or the right-hand grip rule do not register which belongs where.
misconceptions.correction: Using the right hand for the motor effect gives a force in exactly the opposite direction. Left hand for the motor effect; the right-hand rule belongs to induction.

misconceptions.question: How does the resistance of the conductor affect the force on it?
misconceptions.correct: The force depends on the flux density, the current and the length in the field; increasing the resistance reduces the current for a given potential difference, and so reduces the force.
misconceptions.misconception: A higher resistance gives a bigger force, because resistance makes the wire work harder.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Resistance is loosely equated with strength or effort rather than with opposition to current.
misconceptions.correction: Resistance does not appear in F = B I l. Its only influence is through the current: more resistance at the same potential difference means less current, so a smaller force.

misconceptions.question: Does the length of the conductor affect the force on it?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The force is proportional to the length of conductor that is in the magnetic field.
misconceptions.misconception: No, only the current and the strength of the field matter, so the length can be left out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Length looks like a description of the apparatus rather than a physical variable, so it is dropped when the numbers are put into the equation.
misconceptions.correction: Length appears in force = magnetic flux density x current x length. Leaving out a length such as 0.25 m makes the calculated force four times too big.

misconceptions.question: How is the length used in force = magnetic flux density x current x length?
misconceptions.correct: It is multiplied by the flux density and the current.
misconceptions.misconception: You divide by the length, because the force is really a force per metre of wire.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Many quantities met earlier, such as density, speed and resistivity, are per unit quantities obtained by dividing, so dividing feels like the safe operation.
misconceptions.correction: The equation is a product of all three quantities. Doubling the length of conductor in the field doubles the force, because twice as much wire is being pushed.

misconceptions.question: How do you find the flux density when the force, the current and the length are given?
misconceptions.correct: Rearrange force = magnetic flux density x current x length to give flux density = force divided by (current x length).
misconceptions.misconception: Just multiply the three numbers in the question together, because that is what the equation says.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is remembered as an instruction to multiply rather than as a relationship that can be rearranged for whichever quantity is unknown.
misconceptions.correction: Only the subject of the equation is found by multiplying. If the force is the quantity given, the equation must be rearranged before substituting, and the answer will be in tesla, not newtons.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of magnetic flux density?
misconceptions.correct: The tesla, T.
misconceptions.misconception: The weber, because that is the unit that goes with magnetic flux.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Flux and flux density are near-identical names, and the weber is heard alongside them.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states magnetic flux density, B, in tesla, T. Any value of B substituted into F = B I l must be in tesla.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of current in F = B I l?
misconceptions.correct: The ampere, A (amp is acceptable for ampere).
misconceptions.misconception: The coulomb, because current is to do with charge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charge and current are closely linked by charge = current x time, and the unit of the one is offered for the other.
misconceptions.correction: The coulomb is the unit of charge; the ampere is the unit of current. Substituting a charge in coulombs instead of a current in amperes gives a meaningless answer.

misconceptions.question: In a motor, how do the forces on the two opposite sides of the coil act?
misconceptions.correct: In opposite directions: one side is pushed up while the other is pushed down, which turns the coil.
misconceptions.misconception: In the same direction, so the whole coil is pushed sideways out of the field.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students apply Fleming's rule once and assume the answer applies to the whole coil, without noticing that the current runs the opposite way along the far side.
misconceptions.correction: The current travels in opposite directions along the two sides, so Fleming's left-hand rule gives opposite forces. A pair of opposite forces on opposite sides produces rotation, not translation.

misconceptions.question: Why does a current-carrying coil rotate in a magnetic field?
misconceptions.correct: Because the forces on its two opposite sides act in opposite directions and turn it.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the two sides of the coil carry current in opposite directions and so repel each other, pushing the coil round.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule that opposite currents repel is remembered from parallel wires and misapplied as the source of the turning effect.
misconceptions.correction: The turning effect comes from the interaction of the coil's current with the magnet's field, not from the sides acting on each other. Remove the magnet and the coil does not turn.

misconceptions.question: What does the split-ring commutator do?
misconceptions.correct: It reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn.
misconceptions.misconception: It keeps the current in the coil flowing steadily in one direction all the way round.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The commutator is remembered as the part that makes the motor run smoothly, and smooth is read as unchanging.
misconceptions.correction: If the current never reversed, the coil would be pushed back the other way once it passed the vertical. Reversing the current every half turn keeps the turning effect acting the same way round.

misconceptions.question: Is the commutator there to convert a.c. into d.c.?
misconceptions.correct: No. It reverses the current in the coil every half turn so that the coil keeps rotating in the same direction.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes, it changes the alternating supply into direct current for the coil.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The commutator does swap the connections periodically, which sounds like the description of a rectifier the student has met elsewhere.
misconceptions.correction: A simple d.c. motor is already supplied with direct current. The commutator's job is the opposite one: it makes the current in the coil alternate, so that the force keeps turning the coil the same way.

misconceptions.question: What is reversed every half turn in a simple d.c. motor?
misconceptions.correct: The direction of the current in the coil.
misconceptions.misconception: The poles of the magnet are swapped over every half turn.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see that something must reverse to keep the rotation going and attach it to the magnet, which is the more obvious source of the field.
misconceptions.correction: The permanent magnet cannot swap its poles. It is the current that is reversed, by the split-ring commutator sliding onto the opposite brush.

misconceptions.question: How does a moving-coil loudspeaker produce sound?
misconceptions.correct: A varying current in a coil in a magnetic field makes the coil and cone vibrate, producing pressure variations in the air.
misconceptions.misconception: The cone vibrates and induces a varying current in the coil, and that is what makes the sound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Loudspeakers and microphones look almost identical inside, so the direction of the energy transfer is reversed.
misconceptions.correction: A loudspeaker converts variations in current in electrical circuits to the pressure variations in sound waves, using the motor effect. A microphone does the reverse, by induction.

misconceptions.question: Which part of a loudspeaker moves?
misconceptions.correct: The coil, which is attached to the cone; the permanent magnet is fixed.
misconceptions.misconception: The permanent magnet moves and shakes the cone.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The magnet is the more obviously magnetic component, so students make it the active part rather than the light coil carrying the current.
misconceptions.correction: The magnet is heavy and clamped in place; the light coil carries the varying current and is free to move, which is why the design is called a moving-coil loudspeaker.

misconceptions.question: The current in a loudspeaker alternates 500 times per second. What is the frequency of the sound?
misconceptions.correct: 500 Hz. The cone completes one vibration for each cycle of the current.
misconceptions.misconception: 1000 Hz, because the cone moves twice in each cycle, once out and once back.
misconceptions.whyItArises: One complete oscillation is counted as two movements, so the frequency is doubled.
misconceptions.correction: Out and back is one complete cycle, not two. The cone follows the current exactly, so the sound has the same frequency as the current driving the coil.

misconceptions.question: What decides the pitch of the sound from a loudspeaker?
misconceptions.correct: The frequency of the current in the coil; the size of the current decides the loudness.
misconceptions.misconception: The size of the current decides the pitch, and how fast it alternates decides the loudness.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Frequency and amplitude are both properties of the same varying current, and students attach them to the wrong properties of the sound.
misconceptions.correction: Bigger current means a bigger force, so a larger cone movement and a louder sound. More rapid alternation means a higher frequency of vibration and so a higher pitch.

mcqs.stem: A long straight vertical wire carries a steady current. What is the shape of the magnetic field pattern around the wire?

options.text: Circles centred on the wire, in a plane at right angles to it
options.rationale: The field around a straight current-carrying wire is a set of concentric circles lying at right angles to the wire.

options.text: Straight lines spreading outwards from the wire like wheel spokes
options.rationale: A student who pictures a radial pattern, as for light from a lamp, draws lines pointing away from the wire.

options.text: Straight lines running parallel to the wire along its whole length
options.rationale: A student who gives the field the same direction as the current draws it along the wire.

options.text: Loops that leave one end of the wire and re-enter at the other end
options.rationale: This is the bar-magnet pattern, which belongs to a solenoid rather than to a single straight wire.

mcqs.stem: A plotting compass is 2 cm from a straight wire carrying a steady current. It is then moved to 6 cm from the same wire, with the current unchanged. What happens to the magnetic field strength at the compass?

options.text: It stays the same, because only the current sets the field strength
options.rationale: A student who treats current as the only variable sees no change when the current is unchanged.

options.text: It stays the same, because the field is uniform all around the wire
options.rationale: A student who imports uniform from the inside of a solenoid expects the same strength at every point.

options.text: It increases, because the field lines spread apart and overlap there
options.rationale: A student who reads wider spacing as more field lines present concludes that the field builds up further out.

options.text: It decreases, because field strength falls as distance from the wire rises
options.rationale: Field strength depends on the current through the wire and the distance from the wire; only the distance has changed, and it has increased.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the magnetic field inside a long current-carrying solenoid?

options.text: It is zero, because the fields of the turns cancel one another out
options.rationale: A student who notices that opposite sides carry opposite currents wrongly expects the fields to cancel.

options.text: It is circular, forming rings around the axis of the solenoid
options.rationale: A student who carries the single-wire pattern into the coil draws rings inside the solenoid.

options.text: It is strong and uniform, with parallel, evenly spaced field lines
options.rationale: The specification states that the magnetic field inside a solenoid is strong and uniform; parallel evenly spaced lines are how a uniform field is drawn.

options.text: It is strong at the ends but almost zero along the central axis
options.rationale: A student who associates strength with poles puts the field at the ends and leaves the middle empty.

mcqs.stem: Why does shaping a wire into a solenoid increase the strength of the magnetic field produced by the current?

options.text: The fields from the many turns of wire add together inside the coil
options.rationale: Each turn contributes its own field; inside the coil these point the same way and reinforce, giving a strong uniform field.

options.text: The coiled shape lowers the resistance, so a larger current flows
options.rationale: A student who explains every circuit change through resistance and current picks this.

options.text: The turns of wire store the field between them and release it later
options.rationale: A student who treats magnetic field as a substance that can be collected chooses a storage explanation.

options.text: Coiling the wire raises the potential difference across the wire
options.rationale: A student looking for an electrical cause reaches for potential difference, which coiling does not change.

mcqs.stem: The magnetic field around the outside of a current-carrying solenoid is most similar to the field around which of these?

options.text: A straight current-carrying wire, with circles wrapped round the coil
options.rationale: A student who keeps the single-wire pattern in mind draws circles around the coil instead of a bar-magnet field.

options.text: A bar magnet, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other
options.rationale: The specification states that the magnetic field around a solenoid has a similar shape to that of a bar magnet.

options.text: Nothing at all: outside a solenoid there is no magnetic field to speak of
options.rationale: A student who has learned that the field inside is strong assumes all of it is inside.

options.text: A horseshoe magnet, whose field exists only in the gap between the poles
options.rationale: A student who has only seen field diagrams of the gap of a horseshoe magnet transfers that limited picture.

mcqs.stem: An iron core is pushed into the middle of a current-carrying solenoid. What is the effect on the field, and what is the device now called?

options.text: The field becomes stronger, and the device is now a permanent magnet
options.rationale: A student who knows the field grows but thinks the magnetised iron keeps its magnetism names it a permanent magnet.

options.text: The field is unchanged, and the device is still just a plain solenoid
options.rationale: A student who reads the core as a mechanical support expects no magnetic change.

options.text: The field becomes weaker, and the device is called a shielded solenoid
options.rationale: A student who has met iron used as magnetic shielding assumes the core must reduce the field outside.

options.text: The field becomes stronger, and the device is called an electromagnet
options.rationale: Adding an iron core increases the strength of the magnetic field of a solenoid, and an electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core.

mcqs.stem: Which observation best demonstrates that a current in a wire produces a magnetic field?

options.text: The wire becomes warm to the touch when the current is switched on
options.rationale: A student who does not separate the effects of a current offers the heating effect as evidence.

options.text: A plotting compass near the wire deflects when the current is switched on
options.rationale: A compass needle responds only to a magnetic field, so its deflection is direct evidence of the magnetic effect.

options.text: A lamp in series with the wire lights when the current is switched on
options.rationale: A student who treats evidence of current as evidence of a field picks the lamp.

options.text: The reading on the ammeter rises when the potential difference is raised
options.rationale: A student who looks for a measurement rather than a magnetic response chooses the ammeter.

mcqs.stem: The current in a straight vertical wire is reversed. What happens to the magnetic field around the wire?

options.text: The field lines keep their direction but become straight, not circular
options.rationale: A student who ties the field direction to the current direction expects the pattern itself to change.

options.text: The field lines keep both their shape and their direction, as before
options.rationale: A student who thinks only the size of the current matters sees no change at all.

options.text: The field lines keep their circular shape but their direction reverses
options.rationale: Reversing the current reverses the direction in which the circular field lines run, as the right-hand grip rule shows.

options.text: The field lines vanish until the current is switched the original way
options.rationale: A student who thinks the field only exists for one direction of current expects it to switch off.

mcqs.stem: Looking directly at one end of an air-cored solenoid, the conventional current in the coils is seen to run anticlockwise. Which pole faces the observer?

options.text: A north pole, because the current seen from that end runs anticlockwise
options.rationale: Viewed end-on, an anticlockwise conventional current gives a north pole at that end; the field lines emerge towards the observer.

options.text: A south pole, because current flows from north to south inside a coil
options.rationale: A student who applies the field rule to the current instead assigns the poles from the current direction.

options.text: A north pole, because the current enters the coil at that end of the wire
options.rationale: A student who uses an entry-and-exit rule gets the right answer here for the wrong reason.

options.text: Neither pole, because a solenoid has poles only when it has an iron core
options.rationale: A student who associates poles with iron rather than with the field denies the coil any poles.

mcqs.stem: A relay is drawn with a coil, a pivoted iron armature and a pair of contacts in a second circuit. How does the relay work?

options.text: The coil heats a bimetallic strip until it bends across onto the contacts
options.rationale: A student who recalls thermostats offers a heating mechanism for any automatic switch.

options.text: The coil becomes an electromagnet and pulls an iron armature onto the contacts
options.rationale: Current in the coil makes an electromagnet; the field attracts the iron armature, which closes the contacts of the second circuit.

options.text: The coil pushes its current straight into the second circuit, switching it
options.rationale: A student who thinks the two circuits must be joined electrically chooses a direct connection.

options.text: A permanent magnet inside the coil repels the armature onto the contacts
options.rationale: A student who knows magnetism is involved but not that the coil itself is the magnet reaches for a permanent magnet.

mcqs.stem: A wire carrying a current is placed between the poles of a magnet, at right angles to the field. Which statement about the forces is correct?

options.text: Only the wire feels a force; the magnet feels none
options.rationale: A student who watches only the wire jump in the demonstration concludes the magnet is unaffected.

options.text: The magnet and the wire exert a force on each other
options.rationale: In the motor effect the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other; the forces are a Newton's third law pair.

options.text: No force acts unless the wire is already moving
options.rationale: A student who confuses the motor effect with induction thinks movement must come first.

options.text: Only the magnet feels a force; the wire feels none
options.rationale: A student who thinks the magnet is the source of all magnetic behaviour puts the force on it alone.

mcqs.stem: A current-carrying wire is laid along the direction of a uniform magnetic field, parallel to the field lines. What force acts on the wire?

options.text: The largest possible force, because it lies along the field lines
options.rationale: A student who pictures wire and field lining up as maximum interaction chooses the largest force.

options.text: A force of size B I l, acting along the magnetic field lines
options.rationale: A student who expects the force to act along the field applies the equation and gives it that direction.

options.text: No force, because the wire is not at right angles to the field
options.rationale: The force is greatest when the conductor is at right angles to the field and falls to zero when the conductor lies along the field lines.

options.text: A force of size B I l, acting at right angles to the current
options.rationale: A student who applies the equation without checking the right-angle condition still gets a value from it.

mcqs.stem: Fleming's left-hand rule is used with the thumb and first two fingers held at right angles. What does each digit represent?

options.text: Thumb: current; first finger: force (motion); second finger: field
options.rationale: A student who has lost the mnemonic often puts the current on the thumb, the digit named first.

options.text: Thumb: force (motion); first finger: current; second finger: field
options.rationale: A student who swaps the two fingers keeps the thumb right but reverses the predicted force.

options.text: Thumb: force (motion); first finger: field; second finger: current
options.rationale: First finger Field, seCond finger Current, thuMb Motion, using the left hand for the motor effect.

options.text: Thumb: field; first finger: current; second finger: force (motion)
options.rationale: A student who has memorised three words in the wrong order assigns all three quantities incorrectly.

mcqs.stem: A horizontal wire runs from west to east between the poles of a magnet. The magnetic field is horizontal and points from south to north, and the conventional current in the wire flows from west to east. In which direction is the force on the wire?

options.text: Vertically downwards, at right angles to both of them
options.rationale: A student who uses the right hand instead of the left gets a force in exactly the opposite direction.

options.text: Vertically upwards, at right angles to both of them
options.rationale: With the first finger pointing north and the second finger pointing east, the left hand's thumb points vertically upwards.

options.text: Horizontally northwards, along the magnetic field lines
options.rationale: A student who expects the force to act along the field gives the field's own direction.

options.text: Horizontally eastwards, along the current in the wire
options.rationale: A student who expects the wire to be pushed the way its current flows gives the current's direction.

mcqs.stem: Which change would increase the size of the force on a current-carrying conductor placed at right angles to a magnetic field?

options.text: Increasing the current in the conductor
options.rationale: Force = magnetic flux density x current x length, so a larger current gives a larger force.

options.text: Increasing the resistance of the conductor
options.rationale: A student who equates resistance with strength expects more resistance to give more force.

options.text: Reducing the conductor's length in the field
options.rationale: A student who does not treat length as a variable may even expect a shorter wire to concentrate the force.

options.text: Turning the conductor to lie along the field
options.rationale: A student who thinks alignment maximises the interaction expects this to increase the force.

mcqs.stem: A wire of length 0.25 m carries a current of 4.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.30 T. Use force = magnetic flux density x current x length to calculate the force on the wire.

options.rationale: This is 0.30 x 4.0, obtained by leaving the length out of the calculation.
This is 0.30 x 4.0 divided by 0.25, obtained by dividing by the length instead of multiplying.
This is 0.30 x 0.25, obtained by omitting the current from the calculation.

mcqs.stem: In the equation F = B I l, which list gives the units of F, B, I and l in that order?

options.text: newton, weber, ampere, metre
options.rationale: A student who confuses magnetic flux with magnetic flux density gives the weber for B.

options.text: newton, tesla, coulomb, metre
options.rationale: A student who confuses charge with current gives the coulomb for I.

options.text: joule, tesla, ampere, metre
options.rationale: A student who slips between force and energy gives the joule for F.

options.text: newton, tesla, ampere, metre
options.rationale: The specification gives force in newtons, magnetic flux density in tesla, current in amperes and length in metres.

mcqs.stem: A conductor of length 0.40 m carries a current of 5.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field. The force on the conductor is 1.0 N. Calculate the magnetic flux density of the field.

options.rationale: This is 1.0 divided by 5.0, obtained by leaving the length out of the rearranged equation.
This is 1.0 x 5.0 x 0.40, obtained by multiplying the three given values instead of rearranging.
This is 1.0 divided by 0.40, obtained by omitting the current from the rearranged equation.

mcqs.stem: In a simple d.c. electric motor, why does the current-carrying coil turn in the magnetic field?

options.text: The forces on the two opposite sides act in the very same direction
options.rationale: A student who applies Fleming's rule only once assumes both sides are pushed the same way.

options.text: The two sides of the coil repel one another and push the coil round
options.rationale: A student who recalls that opposite currents repel makes the sides act on each other.

options.text: The coil is attracted to the nearer pole and swings towards the magnet
options.rationale: A student who reduces the motor effect to ordinary magnetic attraction expects the coil to be pulled across.

options.text: The forces on the two opposite sides act in opposite directions
options.rationale: The current runs in opposite directions along the two sides, so Fleming's left-hand rule gives opposite forces, which turn the coil.

mcqs.stem: What is the job of the split-ring commutator in a simple d.c. motor?

options.text: It reverses the poles of the field magnet every half turn
options.rationale: A student who knows something must reverse attaches the reversal to the magnet instead of the current.

options.text: It reverses the current in the coil every half turn
options.rationale: Reversing the current every half turn keeps the force on each side of the coil turning it the same way round.

options.text: It keeps the current in the coil steady at all times
options.rationale: A student who reads smooth running as unchanging current chooses a steadying role.

options.text: It turns the alternating input supply into direct current
options.rationale: A student who confuses the commutator with a rectifier reverses the direction of its action.

mcqs.stem: How does a moving-coil loudspeaker produce sound?

options.text: A varying current in a coil in a magnetic field makes the cone vibrate
options.rationale: The motor effect gives a varying force on the coil, so the attached cone vibrates and produces pressure variations in the air.

options.text: A vibrating cone induces a varying current in the coil of the speaker
options.rationale: A student who confuses a loudspeaker with a microphone reverses the direction of the energy transfer.

options.text: A varying magnetic field moves the permanent magnet, shaking the cone
options.rationale: A student who makes the magnet the moving part chooses this.

options.text: A varying current heats the coil, and the air around the coil expands
options.rationale: A student who defaults to the heating effect of a current offers expansion of air as the source of sound.

mcqs.stem: The current supplied to a pair of headphones alternates 500 times each second. What is the frequency of the sound produced?

options.text: 1000 Hz, because the cone moves twice in each cycle of current
options.rationale: A student who counts out and back as two vibrations doubles the frequency.

options.text: It depends on the size of the current, not on how fast it changes
options.rationale: A student who swaps the roles of frequency and amplitude links pitch to the size of the current.

options.text: 500 Hz, because the cone vibrates once per cycle of the current
options.rationale: Each cycle of the current drives one complete out-and-back movement of the diaphragm, so the sound has the same frequency.

options.text: 250 Hz, because the cone is pushed out on only half of each cycle
options.rationale: A student who thinks only the outward push makes sound halves the frequency.
